narrative: The model estimates a 37% probability that you will fail your final year, and this level of risk is why you are being required to take remedial courses. The strongest reason for this prediction is your history of past class failures: you have one previous failure, while students who passed typically have none. This single factor pushes the prediction toward failing more than any other. Two other factors work in your favor. Your family size of three or fewer is the second most influential feature, and it nudges the prediction toward passing, even though only about a third of passing students come from such small families. Your wish to pursue higher education is the third most important factor and also reduces your risk, although all students who passed share that goal. Because the past failure signal is so strong, it outweighs these protective factors. To improve your chances, focus on what you can control: increase your weekly study time from under two hours (most passing students study two to five hours), actively seek help from teachers or family support, and keep your attendance perfect—you currently have zero absences, which is better than the average passer. Remedial courses can help you build the study habits and subject knowledge to turn this risk around.
